These are typically dehydration to eliminate water; acid gas removal for CO and H S; and mercury removal to prevent corrosion of 2 2 aluminum-containing equipment and heavy hydrocarbon stripping. Also, nitrogen or other inert gases are stripped out to get certain LNG product grades. Steps involved in the liquefaction process of natural gas to produce LNG are shown in Figure 36. 56 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 36. LNG liquefaction process. Adapted from Cameron LNG (2018) After precooling the natural gas, it passes through the main cryogenic heat exchanger. There, the gas is cooled to extremely low temperatures and liquefied, typically between −150°C (123 K) and −162°C (111 K), with a mixed refrigerant serving as the refrigerant fluid. Before this process, the mixed refrigerant is precooled and separated under high pressure into vapor and liquid streams. These are then guided through individual tube circuits within the main cryogenic heat exchanger, where each goes through additional cooling, condensing, and deep subcooling. Afterward, the two streams are expanded to a lower pressure, which causes an even further decrease in temperature. As the mixed refrigerant is vaporized in the main cryogenic heat exchanger shell side, it absorbs heat from the process streams and supplies the refrigeration needed for subcooling and liquefaction of the natural gas. During discharge of the main cryogenic heat exchanger and storage in the LNG tanks, some of the liquefied gas flashes to vapor to produce flash gas and boil-off gas. This boil-off gas is used as a fuel to power the gas turbines that power the propane and mixed refrigerant compression cycles that are part of the total liquefaction process. 57 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 37. Cross-sectional view of an LNG storage tank Source: Khan et al. (2020) The LNG is then kept stored in highly specialized full-containment tanks as shown in Figure 37. The pressure inside the tanks is maintained above atmospheric pressure to prevent air from leaking into the tank, which can cause a flammable mixture. A two-layer, full-containment design includes an inner vessel for the LNG itself that is constructed using a nickel-steel alloy capable of withstanding the extremely low temperatures of cryogenic storage. The inner vessel is surrounded by a robust outer tank made of prestressed concrete with a reinforced base and top as an additional containment barrier against leaks or loss of the product. Heavy insulation consisting of perlite powder is used between and around the tank layers to keep the LNG at a stable temperature condition of −160°C (113 K). The storage tanks are usually fitted with a monitoring and protection system that monitors the internal temperature, pressure, liquid level, and any signs of leak. These automated systems play an essential role in maintaining safe operational conditions and minimizing the scope of environmental or operational hazards
